messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Driving with Others: Driving with people
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Marisol had been 20 when the collision happened, riding home in the passenger seat after a long evening shift, still in her work clothes and tired enough that she barely remembered the first stretch of the drive. Then, at an intersection she would later replay over and over, another car entered too fast and struck theirs hard enough to throw her body forward and sideways in one brutal jolt. She remembered the sharp, metallic sound, the sudden loss of control, and the awful realization that for a moment she could not tell where her own body ended and the wreck began. In the weeks after, while the bruising faded and the visible injuries healed, she kept returning to the scene in her mind with a kind of grim exactness. What stayed with her most was not only the impact itself but the sense that the event had been arbitrary and deeply unfair, that something so dangerous had happened in an instant and no one had done anything to prevent it.

Before the crash, Marisol had been straightforward and practical, someone who liked work she could see and measure. She had already been building her life around her trade as an electrician, learning to move confidently through job sites, attics, and cramped spaces. After the collision, though, she found herself looking at her own body differently. She said she no longer trusted it in the same way, and that feeling showed up in the ordinary moments of the day: she would notice a sudden ache, a quickened heartbeat, or a flash of dizziness and immediately wonder whether her body might fail her without warning. Even when she was physically safe, there was a sense of having to stay alert to her own reactions, as if her body had become something less dependable than it had been before.

Driving became one of the first places where the memory pressed in on her. Being in a car with other people was especially difficult, not because she feared the people themselves, but because sitting beside someone else in traffic returned her to the helplessness of the crash. If another vehicle drifted too closely or a car was hit in a parking lot or at an intersection, she would feel the scene seize on her attention with startling force. She described those moments as if the wreck were not fully in the past but arriving again in the present, the image of cars hitting by accident coming with the same hard shock she felt the day of the collision. Even brief rides with coworkers or friends could leave her tense and preoccupied, scanning the road and bracing for the possibility that she would once again be trapped in a situation she could not control.

Over time, Marisol also became wary of anything that pushed her to think too far ahead. Conversations about the future, which had once seemed ordinary, now carried a strange weight. When family members asked about where she saw herself in a year, or when someone at work talked about long-term plans, she often felt her mind tighten around the question. She had come to believe that she could not trust herself to do the right thing when it mattered most, and that uncertainty made even simple planning feel exposed. She worried that if something sudden happened again, she might not respond correctly, might not protect herself or others, and might be left with the same helplessness all over again. That self-doubt was not abstract; it colored the way she spoke about choices, work tasks, and even small decisions that required confidence.

At work, Marisol tried to keep functioning. As an electrician, she still had to move between sites, ride with others to jobs, and step into days that demanded concentration. But the daily environment also held reminders she could not always predict. A drive to a worksite with a crew member could become difficult if traffic slowed or if she happened to see a car with visible damage on the roadside. She learned to sit quietly and focus on objects near her hands or the floor of the vehicle, hoping to get through the ride without the picture of metal crushing metal rising in her mind. The effort of staying composed took a toll in its own way, and there were times she felt pulled back from others because she did not want to explain why these situations were suddenly so hard.

By the time she sought help, Marisol had been carrying these experiences for months and was tired of feeling that the accident had left her life smaller and more fragile. What brought her in was not a single dramatic moment, but the accumulation of tension around driving, the repeated return of crash images when she saw cars hit by accident, and the way talk of the future seemed to unsettle her almost immediately. She wanted relief from the sense that her body could not be trusted and from the anger that what happened to her had been so unfair and had gone unanswered. What she hoped for, even if she did not know exactly how to get there, was a way to feel safe enough in her own life again to ride in a car, keep working, and think about the future without feeling it collapse into the moment of impact.
